# Choosing a local model for this machine

Short answer: start with a 7–8B model at `Q4_K_M`, measure, and only move up if
the quality gap is one you can actually name. Everything below is the reasoning,
and the numbers are worked for a 16 GB card.

The paragraph above is deliberately hard-wrapped at seventy-odd columns, the way
almost every model writes prose, and it must read as **one paragraph** — not as
four short lines with ragged endings.

## What decides the answer

Three quantities, in the order they bind:

1. **VRAM.** Weights, KV cache and the runtime's own overhead all come out of
   the same budget.
2. **Context length.** The KV cache grows linearly with it, and at 32k it can
   outweigh the model.
3. **What you are actually asking for.** Summarising a diff and writing one are
   not the same job.

### The arithmetic

A rule of thumb that has held up:

- weights ≈ *parameters* × *bits per weight* ÷ 8
- KV cache ≈ 2 × *layers* × *context* × *heads* × *head dim* × *bytes*
- leave ~1 GB for the runtime, more if you are also driving a display
  - on Windows, the desktop compositor is not free
  - on Linux with no X session running, it very nearly is

So an 8B model at four bits is about **4.5 GB** of weights, and the cache is what
decides whether 32k context fits beside it.

> Quantisation is lossy, and it is lossy *unevenly*. A model that still writes
> fluent prose at `Q3` may have quietly lost the ability to emit valid JSON.
>
> Test the capability you need, not the capability that is easy to eyeball.

## Reading the quantisation labels

| Label | Bits/weight | 8B weights | Where it breaks first |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | :--- |
| `Q8_0` | 8.5 | 8.5 GB | nothing — it is the reference |
| `Q6_K` | 6.6 | 6.6 GB | nothing you will notice |
| `Q5_K_M` | 5.7 | 5.7 GB | long-chain arithmetic |
| `Q4_K_M` | 4.9 | 4.9 GB | structured output, tool arguments |
| `Q3_K_M` | 3.9 | 3.9 GB | instruction following, JSON validity |

## Wiring it into Vela

Point Vela at the runtime's OpenAI-compatible endpoint. No key is needed and
none is asked for — `llama-server` does not authenticate by default, and *"no
API key"* is a first-class state here, not a warning.

```bash
llama-server \
  --model ./qwen3-8b-q4_k_m.gguf \
  --ctx-size 32768 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8033 \
  --jinja
```

Then add `http://127.0.0.1:8033/v1` as an endpoint and press **Check** to probe
what it can do. The capability row that matters most is `tools`: without
`--jinja` the server will answer a tool request with ~~an error~~ plain prose,
which Vela will show you as a degradation rather than silently swallowing.

### If the probe disagrees with the model card

Believe the probe. A card describes a *model*; the probe describes the
**server** in front of it, and that is the thing you are actually talking to.
See the [llama.cpp server documentation](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp)
for the flags that change the answer.

---

#### One last thing

Run the thing you intend to run, on the machine you intend to run it on, before
you decide what it is worth. Every number above is a starting point for a
measurement, and none of them is a substitute for one.

# Reading a capability report end to end

This document exists to be *looked at*. Every heading level from one to six
appears below, each one immediately followed by prose and by a **bold run** of
its own, because the question it was written to answer cannot be answered from
source: does the type scale still say something true about structure once you
get past the third level, and does the document's own emphasis stay quieter
than the document's own headings?

That gap is not hypothetical. No artifact in the previous evidence set rendered
an `h1`, `h3`, `h4`, `h5` or `h6` at all, so the finding that the scale
collapsed below `h3` — and that an unclassed **bold run** outweighed every
heading under it — had to be read out of a stylesheet rather than seen. A
prompt that emits every level is now part of the set.

## Two — a section

A section heading opens a part of the answer, and a reader skimming for the
part they need should be able to find this line without reading the paragraph
under it. **This bold run sits in the same paragraph**, and it must read as
emphasis inside prose rather than as a heading of its own.

### Three — a sub-section

Three levels down is where model output actually lives: a numbered plan, a
comparison, a set of options. The size step from two to three has to survive
being seen at a glance, next to **a bold run at body size** that is competing
with it for the reader's eye.

#### Four — a sub-sub-section

This is the level the scale used to lose. It sat at exactly body size, at a
weight an unclassed **bold run** beat outright, which meant a fourth-level
heading read as *less* structural than a phrase somebody emphasised in passing.
Size alone cannot separate this level from the one above it — the steps would
be too fine to see — so it has to be separated by something else.

##### Five — a labelled group

Rare in real answers and common in generated outlines. It has to remain
recognisable as a heading while being unmistakably deeper than the level above
it, and it must still outrank **a bold run** sitting directly beside it.

###### Six — the deepest label

The last level stops being a heading-by-size and becomes a label. It is the one
that could otherwise be mistaken for the level above, so it carries its own
case and its own colour, and even here **a bold run** in the paragraph beneath
must not be the loudest thing in view.

## Back up to two, to prove the rhythm resets

Vertical rhythm is half of a heading scale: space above a heading binds it to
what follows and separates it from what came before. A document that returns to
a second-level heading after a sixth-level one should visibly *reopen*, not
merely continue. If every level carries the same margin, the whole answer reads
as one flat list of equals no matter what the sizes say.

Below the fold there is ordinary prose, long enough to measure a line against:
a comfortable reading measure is sixty-five to seventy-five characters, and a
column that sets ninety-five to a hundred and five is the difference between an
answer you read and an answer you skim and give up on. The paragraph you are
reading is deliberately hard-wrapped in its source at seventy-odd columns, the
way almost every model writes prose, and it must reflow to *your* column rather
than keeping the model's line endings.

**Deconstruct the requirements:**

*   The user wants a *model-agnostic* client, so the answer
    cannot name a vendor.
*   They mentioned `llama-server`, which means the endpoint is
    OpenAI-compatible.

Answering now.
